newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian government says 300 Khmer Rouge defect.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian government says 300 Khmer Rouge defect.

text.p: Some 300 Khmer Rouge guerrillas have defected to the government from bases on the northwest shore of Cambodia's Tonle Sap, or Great Lake, senior army commanders said on Tuesday.

Seng Huot, commander of the fighters, told reporters his regiment had previously followed former top Khmer Rouge cadre Ieng Sary but was not prepared to wait further for the dissident leader and his commanders to join forces with the government.
Reporters met more than 100 of the defectors at Prek Narin, a village some 20 km (12 miles) north of Cambodia's second largest city, Battambang.

The men from Regiment 408, wearing a motley assortment of outfits and carrying assorted weapons, were brought to the village on Monday for a national reconciliation ceremony and to receive government uniforms and assistance.

Royal army officers said the former rebels had begun joining the government unconditionally on Sunday and were not linked to Ieng Sary, who broke from the mainstream Khmer Rouge in August and forged a ceasefire with the army.
Ieng Sary was foreign minister in the brutal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot and was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide of more than one million people.

King Norodom Sihanouk granted him an amnesty on September 14, paving the way for talks on a military merger. The government has turned down demands for top central command posts but is ready to offer senior regional military positions.
Government officials have insisted that Ieng Sary's forces merge immediately with the government.

General Preap Pan, deputy commander of regional forces, said it was the first time Khmer Rouge guerrillas had defected from areas close to the vast inland lake, from where they had posed a threat to traffic along national highway five linking Phnom Penh to Battambang and the northwest.

"The Khmer Rouge defectors said they are coming here without conditions. They said they are different from other the other guerrillas in (Phnom) Malai and Pailin," the general said, referring to the two main bases under Ieng Sary's control.

The government was to hand over 600 uniforms, 10 tonnes of rice and 70 tents to the fighters and their families, officers said, adding that they could keep their current ranks when they joined the army.
Some guerrillas said recent flooding had exacerbated the hardships of everyday life. "There have been floods for more than 10 days, and we have no homes," said 32-year-old Seng Sary.
The Khmer Rouge signed a U.N.-brokered peace accord with rival factions in 1991 but later reneged on the pact. They had been fighting the coalition government that emerged from the elections in 1993.
